analysis.one_liner: Taxes drugmakers up to 100% of revenue from price increases that outpace inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Rep. Mark Pocan with one cosponsor in February 2019, was referred to two House committees and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have hit pharmaceutical companies with an excise tax of 50% to 100% on the extra revenue they earn whenever they raise a prescription drug's price faster than inflation. Companies would have had to report prices and revenues to the HHS Inspector General every quarter, and the findings would be published online. Money collected would fund NIH drug research, and a government study would examine how new-drug launch prices are set.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients, taxpayers, and insurers who pay for prescription drugs would benefit, because the tax makes outsized price increases immediately expensive for the manufacturer rather than profitable. Insulin-style spike-and-jump pricing would be taxed at up to 100% of the extra revenue, and the cumulative tax would catch companies that raise prices a little each year so they add up to a large total. The public also gains transparency: the Inspector General's findings on each price spike, with the company's rationale, would be published (trade secrets excluded). Finally, any revenue collected is earmarked to expand National Institutes of Health funding for drug research.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and payers of drug prices

how_it_helps.text: Imposes an excise tax on pharmaceutical companies equal to 50% of the extra revenue from a price increase above inflation (75% for increases of 15-20%, 100% for increases of 20% or more), so large price spikes stop being profitable.

Adds a cumulative tax so companies cannot dodge the rules by raising prices a small amount every year; a drug whose price has climbed well above inflation over two to five years owes tax on the whole accumulated increase.

Requires quarterly public reporting of drug prices, sales, and revenues to the HHS Inspector General, with civil penalties of 0.5-1% of a drug's gross revenue per day for late reports, and publishes the Inspector General's assessment of each price spike and the company's stated rationale (with trade secrets excluded).

Protects legitimate increases: HHS may exempt drugs whose price rose for cause (such as higher input costs), and cheap generic-competitive drugs under $10 for a 30-day supply can be exempted; the bill also explicitly forbids a company from winning an exemption by threatening to curtail production.

Directs that any revenue collected be appropriated to the National Institutes of Health for drug research and development, and requires a Government Accountability Office study of how launch prices for new drugs are set and what alternatives exist.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical companies that raise drug prices faster than inflation would pay the excise tax on the extra revenue from the increase, plus daily penalties for failing to file the required quarterly price reports. To the extent companies respond by moderating price increases, they forgo revenue they would otherwise have collected from patients, insurers, and government health programs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Drugmakers raising prices faster than inflation

drawbacks.text: The tax only reaches price increases after a drug is already on the market; a company can still launch a new drug at a very high price and owe nothing. The bill's own requirement that the GAO study how launch prices are set acknowledges this gap.

Manufacturers might pass some of the tax through in higher prices elsewhere or reduce supply of drugs that become taxable, and the HHS for-cause exemption process gives the Secretary broad discretion that companies would predictably litigate.

The quarterly reporting regime is a real compliance burden: every holder of an approved drug application must file detailed quarterly price, volume, and revenue data to the Inspector General, with penalties accruing daily for late filings.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients and payers the upside is large: a structural penalty on the most notorious drug-pricing behavior, price spikes and small repeated hikes that outpace inflation, plus public disclosure of each company's stated rationale. The design gaps are real but secondary: launch prices escape untouched, some administrative discretion could be gamed or litigated, and the compliance burden falls only on companies that are already marketing federally covered prescription drugs. On balance the costs fall almost entirely on the manufacturers whose pricing the tax targets.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in two House committees from the day it was introduced in February 2019 until the Congress ended in January 2021, with no hearing, no vote, and no floor action.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Pocan introduced the Stop Price Gouging Act on February 7, 2019, joined by Rep. Marcy Kaptur as the bill's only cosponsor.

The House referred it to both the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, and it was also referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee; neither committee took it up.
The bill never advanced past referral: there was no committee markup, no vote in either chamber, and no further action of any kind before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers came out ahead: they never faced the excise tax, the quarterly reporting requirements, or the public disclosure of their pricing rationale, and consumers continued to bear the cost of above-inflation drug price increases.

against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers and their trade associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed excise-tax penalties on drug price increases as part of the industry's broad resistance to drug-pricing legislation during the 116th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, and with only two Democratic sponsors and no Republican support recorded, the bill never developed a partisan profile one way or the other.

industries.note: The bill would tax away 50-100% of the extra revenue from any price increase above inflation, tax cumulative multi-year increases, require quarterly price disclosures, and publish the rationale for each spike. It strikes directly at spike-driven pricing strategies that have been especially profitable for brand-name and legacy drug holders.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employers that pay for drug benefits
industries.note: Payers would benefit indirectly from slower drug price growth; the bill does not regulate insurers, and the GAO study would examine how health plans help set launch prices.
